Microcirculation

Near-infrared exposure increased measured microcirculatory flow in some controlled human studies, including a chronic-wound trial. In a direct comparison, 830-nm near-infrared light increased median flow while 633-nm red light did not. Responses varied, and lasting clinical benefit has not been established.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Near-infrared exposure increased measured microcirculatory flow in some controlled human studies, including a chronic-wound trial. In a direct comparison, 830-nm near-infrared light increased median flow while 633-nm red light did not. Responses varied, and lasting clinical benefit has not been established.

Summary of the Evidence

Fourteen publications are assigned to the microcirculation category. The database classifies eleven human reports, including four randomized studies and seven other reports, alongside three animal studies and one publication with laboratory work. Some method categories overlap. A 2023 human paper is a secondary analysis of the 20-person randomized study published in 2020, so it is not an additional independent cohort. The studies also differ in whether they measured skin flow, wound temperature, oxygenation, or healing.

Human and clinical evidence

In the randomized study of 20 adults, a five-minute near-infrared exposure at 830 nm increased median microcirculatory flow by 27%, rising to 54% during the 20-minute follow-up. The 633-nm red-light arm did not increase median flow. Only half the participants met the study’s response definition, and baseline hand temperature helped distinguish responders from non-responders. The 2023 waveform paper reanalyzed this cohort rather than testing a new group (Gavish et al. 2020 Ovadia-Blechman et al. 2023).

A randomized double-blind study of 79 people with chronic wounds reported increased blood flow in the active LED groups during eight weeks of treatment. Its comparator received broadband light rather than a passive sham, which complicates attribution to PBM alone (Frangez et al. 2017). A sham-controlled study in 30 healthy volunteers found an immediate rise in foot capillary velocity and flow with monochromatic infrared exposure. By contrast, a small study of 11 people found no significant oxygenation change after 635-nm red light. A 2026 single-session study of 20 people with 33 ulcers found a temperature rise in diabetic foot ulcers but not venous ulcers; temperature is an indirect microcirculation measure, not proof of wound healing (Gavish et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

A rabbit experiment reported larger collateral vessels and increased microcirculatory measures after light exposure. A rat wound-healing experiment did not find a significant sustained microcirculatory effect. These different models do not establish how people with vascular disease will respond.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One human microcirculation publication also included an in-vitro component. It is counted within that paper and does not add another clinical cohort. The direct evidence is primarily physiological measurement in people or animals, rather than isolated cell studies.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols ranged from a single five-minute exposure to repeated wound treatment. Tested wavelengths included 633 and 635 nm red visible light and 830, 850, and 890 nm near-infrared light. The 2020 study’s near-infrared arm changed flow while its red arm did not, showing that results from one wavelength should not be assumed for another. Exposure site, baseline temperature, devices, and endpoints also varied. There is no single dose or schedule validated across these conditions.

Interpretation

Controlled human studies reported acute increases in measured microcirculatory flow in some settings. In one randomized comparison, 830-nm near-infrared exposure increased median hand flow, whereas 633-nm red light did not; a chronic-wound study also found increased local flow during LED treatment. Responses differed by person, site, and protocol. The flow changes are measurable but do not establish durable benefit across clinical conditions.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for acute measured flow changes in selected human settings Low for consistent responses across settings or lasting clinical benefit
Publications and records14 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Several controlled human experiments found acute increases in measured flow after near-infrared exposure, including during wound care, while 633-nm red light did not increase median flow in the direct comparison. Responses varied by person and site, and measured changes do not themselves establish durable clinical benefit. Repeated trials linking flow changes to wound healing or symptoms would support a broader rating.
